verdicts.reason: The answer does not identify Lynn Goldsmith as the creator of the Prince photograph or provide any source-supported findings.
The answer supplies no chronology and does not state that the 1981 photograph preceded the 1984 commissioned illustration.
The answer does not describe the limited artist-reference authorization for the 1984 Vanity Fair commission.
The answer does not distinguish the broader Prince Series from the particular Orange Prince image licensed in 2016.
The answer does not identify the later Condé Nast 2016 license or separate it from the 1984 commission.
The answer does not report the $10,000 fee paid to AWF for the challenged 2016 use.
The answer does not state that Goldsmith neither authorized nor was compensated for the challenged 2016 use.
The answer provides no use-specific assessment of the challenged magazine licensing transaction.
The answer does not identify the first fair-use factor, purpose and character, as the issue decided by the Court.
The answer does not explain that transformation must be assessed against the specific alleged infringing use.
The answer does not identify the overlapping purpose of illustrating magazine stories about Prince.
The answer does not account for the commercial licensing character of the challenged transaction.
The answer provides no discussion of commerciality's role and therefore does not substantively explain that it is not an automatic bar.
The answer does not explain how the degree of changed purpose interacts with commerciality and justification.
The answer does not explain that an overbroad new-expression test would swallow the derivative-work right.
The answer does not recognize that creation, display, or other uses may present different first-factor questions.
The answer does not acknowledge that new meaning or message may be relevant to the fair-use analysis.
The answer does not explain why a new message alone did not justify this overlapping commercial license.
The answer does not explain the Campbell parody comparison or its copying-justification reasoning.
The answer does not assess the reason for borrowing this photograph in relation to the asserted purpose.
The answer does not distinguish the functional software context in Google or explain why it does not mechanically control this portrait license.
The answer provides no analysis rejecting artistic fame as an independent fair-use entitlement.
The answer does not state AWF's transformation/new-meaning argument or explain the majority's response.
The answer does not address Goldsmith's competing portrait-licensing purpose while limiting the holding to the challenged use.
The answer does not report that the first factor favored Goldsmith for the challenged use.
The answer does not state that the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment under review.
The answer does not discuss the concurrence's emphasis on the specific challenged use.
The answer does not identify or fairly attribute the dissent's concern for artistic transformation as a dissent.
The answer provides no substantive discussion of the judgment or record and therefore does not fulfill the required treatment of damages/valuation.
The answer does not request the original license scope or sublicensing permissions before clearing a new use.
The answer does not request the proposed medium, audience, commercial terms, or asserted purpose for a license.
The answer gives no conditional options for permission, revised use, or further analysis and does not address clearance at all.
